question: Does the right to privacy under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution extend to digital data protection, and what legal test must state surveillance satisfy to comply with it?
reference_answer: Yes. In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court of India held that the right to privacy is a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21. Any state intrusion into privacy, including digital surveillance, must satisfy a three-fold test: (1) legality (backed by a clear law), (2) necessity (serving a legitimate state aim), and (3) proportionality (proportional relation between the objective and the constraint on the right).

question: Under Regulation 3 and 4 of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations 2015, what constitutes Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI), and can communications be made to joint venture partners during due diligence?
reference_answer: Under the SEBI PIT Regulations, UPSI is any information relating to a company or its securities that is not generally available and which upon becoming available is likely to materially affect the price of the securities. Communication of UPSI is prohibited under Regulation 3 except where it is in furtherance of legitimate purposes, performance of duties, or discharge of legal obligations. Due diligence communication is permitted under Regulation 3(3) subject to executing confidentiality agreements.

question: In the provided lease agreement, the landlord Rajesh Kumar has a clause saying he can issue a cheque bounce notice within 60 days of dishonour. Does this comply with Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act?
reference_answer: No. Under Section 138(b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the payee must make a demand for payment by giving notice in writing within 30 days of receiving the return memo from the bank. Any contract clause extending this statutory notice period to 60 days violates this mandatory statutory limit, rendering the criminal action under Section 138 invalid. In Dalmia Cement (2001), the Supreme Court upheld that statutory timelines under Section 138 must be strictly enforced.
